title: Coastal Wave Blending and Sunset Light in a Multi‑Shot Composite (New Zealand setting reference)

summary: This tutorial-style walkthrough shows how to build a coastal composite by selecting two water-focused shots, aligning them around a shared wave/rock motif, and painting one shot into the other to preserve a distinctive swirl and edge sharpness. The workflow emphasizes exposure matching with a water buffer, masking and brush-based blending to fuse elements, and then shaping tonality before introducing light. The latter section demonstrates creating a sunset-inspired glow using Camera Raw, adding reflected light on wet rocks, and employing dodge and diffusion to control foreground brightness without washing out the sky. Throughout, the presenter reinforces planning the composition around a leading swirl and edge details, while using subtle color and light tweaks to unify the final image. The result is a cohesive coastal scene with a clear foreground primary shot, a detailed secondary contribution, and a warm, sunset-driven background that remains visually balanced.

sections.description: The presenter selects candidate coastal shots, notes wind-induced shakiness in a background shot, and designates a sharp foreground rock with a visible swirl as the primary image. They discuss applying prior settings to additional shots and recognizing that exact exposure alignment isn’t mandatory when a water buffer exists; emphasis is placed on the swirl as a key compositional element and on the leading line to guide the viewer’s eye.

sections.description: Allocation shifts toward aligning the two shots so the wave and rock features line up, then painting in portions of the secondary shot to extend the swirl and maintain edge clarity. The artist notes that exact cross-shot alignment isn’t necessary everywhere—only the salient edges—and demonstrates handling mismatches in mid-ground while keeping distant splashes under control.

sections.description: The final phase focuses on creating a controlled lighting window through tonal shaping, then layering light and color to evoke a fiery sunset. The workflow includes using mid-tone dodge for light placement on water, applying a vignette to center attention, bleeding sunset hues via Camera Raw, and adding warm reflected light on wet rocks. The author stresses avoiding over-brightening the sky and emphasizes the importance of diffusion, shadow-dodging, and selective color tweaks to achieve a cohesive final image.
